title: The Remainder and Factor Theorems
short: p(a) is the remainder when dividing by x − a; p(a) = 0 means x − a is a factor.

blocks.html: After a few synthetic divisions you may notice something: the remainder from dividing by $x - r$ is always $p(r)$. That is not a coincidence, and it gives two powerful shortcuts.
Remainder theorem: when $p(x)$ is divided by $x - r$, the remainder is $p(r)$. Factor theorem: $x - r$ is a factor of $p(x)$ exactly when $p(r) = 0$.

Division always gives $p(x) = (x - r)\,q(x) + R$, where the remainder $R$ is a number because it has lower degree than $x - r$. This is true for every $x$, so put in $x = r$: $p(r) = (r - r)\,q(r) + R = 0 + R = R$. If that remainder is 0, then $p(x) = (x - r)\,q(x)$, which says exactly that $x - r$ is a factor. Graphically, $p(r) = 0$ means the graph crosses or touches the $x$-axis at $r$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $p(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + x + 6$. Drag the point along the graph: its height $p(r)$ is the remainder when you divide by $x - r$. Where the height is 0, $x - r$ is a factor.

blocks.title: A remainder without dividing
blocks.q: Find the remainder when $p(x) = x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5$ is divided by $x - 2$.
steps: By the remainder theorem, it is $p(2)$.

blocks.title: Finding a missing coefficient
blocks.q: Find $k$ so that $x - 2$ is a factor of $x^3 + kx^2 - 4x + 4$.

blocks.html: Evaluating at the wrong sign: for the divisor $x + 1$ you need $p(-1)$, not $p(1)$. The number to use is the one that makes the divisor 0.
